title: Rāgas Especially Suited to the Flute
summary: Rāgas that suit the flute: easy, sweet ones (Bhūpālī, Pahāḍī, Durgā, Mālkauns, Yaman) and sweet but hard ones (Pīlū, Bhairavī, Darbārī, Pūriyā); holes meant to be half-opened are best made oval. Śloka 147 advises staying with one rāga for a long time, as one digs in one spot to reach water.

blocks.text: There are only a few rāgas that can be played easily on the flute (bānsurī) and that are considered the sweetest on the flute, such as Bhūpālī, Pahāḍī, Durgā, Mālkauns and Yaman.

There are also some rāgas which, while sweet, are difficult as well, such as Pīlū, Bhairavī, Darbārī and Pūriyā. In fact, all rāgas are sweet when played with skill. But the rāgas that make an immediate impression on the hearts of ordinary people are all the more praiseworthy. If the flute has eight holes, many rāgas can be played easily by changing the place of 'Sa' again and again. But some particular practitioners (sādhakas) consider doing so a cowardice on their part, so they take 'Sa' at one single place and practise every rāga properly. In this situation, if the flute has eight or nine holes, the practice of lifting a finger halfway has to be done only for 'Re', 'Dha' and śuddha (natural) 'Ma'. Whereas on a flute with six holes, hard practice of lifting a finger halfway, or [opening a hole] halfway, has to be done for the altered forms of all the notes except 'Sa', that is, for komal (flat) and tīvra (sharp). Therefore it is more useful to make the holes that need to be opened half or less than half oval, rather than fully round.

blocks.verse:
जलाभिषाली क्वचिदल्प भूमौ दीर्घेण धैर्येण खनन् यथा हि।
उपैत्यगाधम् सलिलं तथैव कालेन साध्यः खलु राग एकः।१४७।
blocks.text: Just as one who longs for water, digging with long patience in one small piece of ground, reaches deep water, in the same way one rāga is indeed to be mastered over time.

That is, just as a person who wants to find water does not dig a little in many places but digs patiently and long at one single point and reaches deep water, in the same way it is necessary for practitioners (sādhakas) to ripen one single rāga patiently over a long time, and then to transfer whatever mastery (siddhi) has been gained in that rāga to other rāgas, one by one. For a rāga is only a means; what is to be achieved is svara (note) and tāla themselves. If the arrangement of notes is mastered in one rāga, then arrangement of the same level is possible in other rāgas too. Those who learn a different rāga every day gain nothing even after years. Well-wishing gurus give their dear disciple training (tālīm) in one single rāga for two or three years. Therefore in this book too, gats and so on are being written through just one or two rāgas. For other rāgas it will be necessary to consult other books.
